parts.title: A fast, efficient way to teach large language models new jobs
parts.abstract:
Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are computer programs that are very good at many jobs with human language, such as answering questions or translating text. But getting them to work well on a narrow, specialized job, like one used in a particular company or field, takes a lot of resources. Building the examples they need to learn from is costly, and training them on those examples, a step called fine-tuning, needs a lot of computing power. In this work, we propose a complete, end-to-end strategy for fine-tuning LLMs quickly for specialized jobs, even when both the data and the computing power are limited.

Methods

Our strategy uses a method called Distilling Step-by-Step (DSS) both to build the training examples and to train the model. In our task, the model takes a question written in everyday language and turns it into a search command written in a special code called Query DSL. A larger "teacher" model writes the correct answer for each question. It also writes a short step-by-step explanation of how it reached that answer, using a technique called Chain-of-Thought prompting. We then use these answers and explanations as the correct examples for training.

With this training material ready, we tested three ways of fine-tuning. We tried many different settings for each one, a process called a hyperparameter sweep. The three ways are full-precision fine-tuning, which updates the whole model; Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), which adds small extra parts to the model; and Quantized LoRA (QLoRA), which does the same but stores the model's numbers in a more compact form. To find out how much the step-by-step explanations help, we also ran a comparison that left one part out. We compared DSS training, which teaches the model both the answers and the explanations, with training that teaches only the answers.

Results

Across all the setups we tested, DSS combined with full-precision fine-tuning gave the best overall results. When resources are limited, DSS with LoRA offers a good balance between how well the model performs and how much computing it needs. DSS with QLoRA lets us train even when the graphics cards (GPUs) have less memory, while still keeping up with the other methods. For the methods that change only a small part of the model, we found that setting the LoRA "alpha" to four times the "rank" (an alpha-to-rank ratio of 4:1) gave a steady balance between performance and computing cost across the settings we explored.

Discussion

These findings support a practical process for adapting models to specialized jobs when resources are limited. First, use DSS to build the training examples efficiently. Then choose the fine-tuning method based on how much computing you have: full-precision when you can, and LoRA or QLoRA when memory is limited. Our workflow offers a general guide for fine-tuning LLMs efficiently for specialized jobs when little data is available.
parts.introduction_first: Large language models (LLMs) are the best tools we have today for working with human language on computers. They are built on a design called the transformer, a type of neural network (Vaswani et al., 2023). Older methods for handling language relied on simple translation rules and on statistics to predict what comes next in a piece of text (Bengio et al., 2000). The usual way to fine-tune an LLM, which means training it further on new examples, takes a lot of resources and time. That is because building the training examples takes work, and running the training itself takes a lot of computing. In this paper, we introduce a way to build training examples and fine-tune LLMs for specialized jobs, even when there is little data and little computing power. Our approach uses Distilling Step-by-Step (DSS) to build the training examples, with the work spread across several computers working together. We then use this approach as a starting point to compare well-known fine-tuning methods, to find the most efficient one for quickly building models for specialized jobs.
parts.conclusion:
6

Conclusions

Large language models are taking big steps forward in deep learning and in working with human language on computers. In this work, we stress how important it is to fine-tune these models efficiently for specialized jobs that go beyond the data they were first trained on. Two things matter a great deal for whether LLMs are widely used in real-world settings, where they need to be tuned for particular uses. One is how efficiently we can build the training examples for these jobs. The other is how efficiently we can fine-tune the models themselves.

In this study, we offered an efficient strategy for fine-tuning large language models for specific tasks. DSS lets us quickly build training examples that include both the correct answers and the step-by-step explanations. Combining DSS with full-precision fine-tuning gives a complete, end-to-end method. It lets us quickly build and put into use models for specific tasks that perform as well as, or better than, larger models on those tasks.

We also carried out a thorough search of training settings and compared the fine-tuning methods using the FLAN T5 family of models as an example. This shows that, when resources are limited, DSS with LoRA for fine-tuning, using an alpha-to-rank ratio of 4:1, balances performance and computing cost. Where the computing power of the graphics cards (GPUs) is the main concern, DSS with QLoRA for fine-tuning, also with an alpha-to-rank ratio of 4:1, is a strong choice.

Adding these methods to the everyday workflows of real-world use, with many different kinds of LLMs, could greatly reduce the time and cost of building models for specific tasks. That would make it easier to build on these systems and to research how useful they are.
parts.introduction_rest:
Large language models have been shown again and again to be excellent at jobs that involve text. Even so, they have limits that make them harder to use for specialized jobs. One limit is that they are trained on huge collections of everyday text, and these collections often contain little or nothing about specialized fields such as law or medicine (Nori et al., 2023). Because of this missing knowledge, the text an LLM writes can sound sensible but still be wrong (Zhang et al., 2023).

Another limit is size. An LLM is made up of hundreds of millions to hundreds of billions of parameters, which are the adjustable numbers the model learns during training. Models this big need computers with a great deal of computing power. That costs a lot of money, whether the model runs on computers owned by the organization (on-premises) or on rented computers over the internet (cloud computing) (Chen et al., 2023).

Fine-tuning, and related methods, are still the standard way to get a ready-made LLM to work well on a specialized job and to follow the rules that job requires. We summarize earlier research on fine-tuning in Section 2. In this study, we compare full-precision fine-tuning with two methods that change only a small part of the model: LoRA and QLoRA. We do this under limits on the memory of the graphics cards (GPUs), like those found in places with little computing power.

To keep the cost of building the training examples down, we use DSS (Hsieh et al., 2023) to create a set of examples made for our task. Each example includes both the correct answer and the step-by-step explanation. We then run a comparison that leaves one part out, testing training with the explanations against training with the answers only.

As our example model, we use FLAN-T5, in its Small, Base, Large and XL versions. FLAN-T5 is a model that has already been trained to follow instructions. It reads a piece of text and turns it into another piece of text, which makes it a good fit for our task of turning a question into a search command. We use it to see how the results change as we scale up the fine-tuning method, for a task that produces a structured output. We chose FLAN-T5 because it performs strongly on translation tasks and is well suited to turning text into structured output (Wei et al., 2022).

In this work, we describe how we extended the DSS method to the FLAN-T5 models. We then compare how well DSS works alongside the three fine-tuning methods: standard fine-tuning, LoRA and QLoRA. For all of them, we use the new set of training examples that DSS created for our task, which turns everyday-language questions into Query DSL.

DSS gives an efficient way to build training examples that include both the correct answers and the step-by-step explanations. But how much the explanations actually help, compared with training on the answers only, is still an open question about how to do this kind of work. Earlier research has shown that DSS helps models learn more efficiently on open-source benchmark datasets, which are shared collections of test questions (Hsieh et al., 2023). However, no one has yet reported a careful, side-by-side comparison of DSS fine-tuning and training on the answers only, using training examples built for a specific task. This is especially true for methods that change only a small part of the model, and for training with the model's numbers stored in a compact form.

To fill this gap, we designed a comparison that leaves one part out. It tests training with the explanations against training with the answers only, so that we can see the effect of the explanations on its own. We run this comparison across several model sizes and fine-tuning methods. This lets us check whether the help from the explanations changes with how big the model is or with the limits of the training.

Large language models are a major step forward in deep learning and in working with human language on computers. In this work, we stress how important it is to fine-tune these models efficiently for specialized jobs that go beyond the data they were first trained on. Our work offers a guide for fine-tuning LLMs efficiently for specialized jobs when little data is available.

DSS combined with full-precision fine-tuning gave better results. When resources are limited, use LoRA fine-tuning with an alpha-to-rank ratio of 4:1, to balance performance and computing cost. When the memory of the graphics cards is limited, use QLoRA fine-tuning with an alpha-to-rank ratio of 4:1. Our code and instructions are available at this GitHub link: https://github.com/brmarsh23/An-Efficient-Strategy-for-Fine-Tuning-Large-Language-Models.
parts.methods:
3

Materials and methods

3.1

Distilling Step-by-Step

Distilling Step-by-Step (DSS) is a method in which a teacher LLM writes the correct answers for a task and also writes the step-by-step explanations behind them. We then use these to train a smaller model so that it matches how well the teacher does. Earlier work showed that models fine-tuned with DSS perform better than larger models trained with the usual fine-tuning methods. This held both on standard test collections of questions and on few-shot learning tasks, where a model is given only a handful of examples before it has to answer new ones (Hsieh et al., 2023).

To get the step-by-step explanations, we prompted the teacher models with Chain-of-Thought prompting (Wei et al., 2023). This technique makes the model write out its reasoning along the way, which explains how the input connects to the answer (Hsieh et al., 2023). Figure 2 shows an example prompt. The prompt has three parts. Together they tell the model about the DSL interface and about the dataset for the task it will later do, and they encourage the model to reason step by step. The last part, **Question**, holds an example question from a user. Using this prompt layout, we pulled the explanations and the DSL answers out of the teacher model. The answers came as JSON, a standard text format for storing data.

Figure 2

An example prompt. It gives instructions on how to format DSL search commands, describes the dataset for the task, and uses Chain-of-Thought prompting.

Once we had the explanations and answers for every input, we added the explanations to the training examples. To do this, we set up the fine-tuning as a multi-task problem, meaning the model has to do two jobs at once. For each input, we placed a short tag in front of the question. One tag said "rationale" and the other said "label". Each tag matched the kind of output the model should produce, so the student model could tell the two jobs apart. In this way, the student model learned to produce the correct explanations and answers for each input.

3.2

The training dataset

We built a training dataset for one job: turning questions written in everyday language into Query DSL. Query DSL is a flexible search language that the OpenSearch data-analysis platform uses to search through databases (Contributors, 2024). Teaching a language model to do this translation would let people work with databases in a more conversation-like way, and so lead to wider use.

The dataset contained 1000 questions in everyday language, each to be translated into Query DSL for searching the OpenSearch database. Each question was paired with two outputs. The first was the correct answer: a properly formatted Query DSL object written in JSON, which would give the OpenSearch results the question was asking for. The second was the explanation, which described in a short, step-by-step way how to build that JSON. Figure 3 shows an example of how an explanation and answer were made for one input. Figure 4 shows an example of a training step using the answers and explanations. We made both the answers and the explanations as described in the previous subsection. For the teacher model we used Mixtral 8x22B, an open-source LLM of the Sparse Mixture of Experts (MOE) type (Team, 2024). In total, the dataset had 1000 questions, each with a matching pair of answer and explanation, and we used the whole dataset for fine-tuning.

Figure 3

How we built the dataset with DSS. Chain-of-Thought prompting pulls the explanations and answers out of the teacher model. Here, the Mixtral 8x22B LLM was the teacher model.

Figure 4

An example training step using a dataset made with DSS. A tag (rationale or label) is placed in front of the input, and the student model is trained to produce the output that matches that tag.

3.3

The model designs

Table 1 shows the different designs of the FLAN T5 model that we used. They differ in several key ways. The most important is the total number of parameters, which are the adjustable numbers inside the model that it learns. This number depends on three things. The first is how many layers the model has, both in its encoder and its decoder. The second is the size of the feedforward layers, which are the layers that do the main calculations. The third is how many attention heads each attention block has, in each encoder and decoder layer. Attention heads are small parts that let the model focus on the most relevant words in a sentence.

Going from FLAN T5 Small to T5 Base to T5 Large, the feedforward layers get bigger, the number of layers goes up, and the number of attention heads goes up. As a result, the total number of parameters rises steadily as the model gets bigger. FLAN T5 XL is different. Its feedforward layers have four times as many parameters as those of FLAN T5 Large, and each attention block has twice as many attention heads. This makes FLAN T5 XL much bigger than FLAN T5 Large. In this work, we used the FLAN T5 Small, Base, Large, and XL designs to see how well and how efficiently the three fine-tuning methods (full-precision, LoRA, and QLoRA) work on the Query DSL dataset.

Table 1

The FLAN T5 model designs used in this work.

| Model | Parameters | Layers | Size | Heads

| FLAN T5 Small | 76.956 | 6 | 2,048 | 8

| FLAN T5 Base | 247.577 | 12 | 3,072 | 12

| FLAN T5 Large | 770.567 | 24 | 4,096 | 16

| FLAN T5 XL | 2,884.497 | 24 | 16,384 | 32

Model size is in millions of parameters. Layers is the number of encoder and decoder layers in each model. Size is the size of the linear (feedforward) layers. Heads is the number of attention heads in each attention block.

3.4

The fine-tuning methods

Fine-tuning means taking a language model that has already been trained and training it on extra tasks, using a smaller set of examples than it was first trained on. The classic way to do this is to make some or all of the model's parameters free to change. The model stores these parameters as numbers, called weights, and we keep them in full floating-point precision, which is the standard, most exact form. We then train the weights using a lower learning rate than the one used during the original training. The learning rate controls how big a step the model takes each time it adjusts itself. In this work, we call this classic method full-precision fine-tuning. It can work very well, but it costs a lot of computing, especially GPU memory (Quentin and Stella Biderman, 2023). Because of this high cost, people have developed efficient methods that balance cost and performance. We tested two of them, LoRA and QLoRA, alongside full-precision fine-tuning (see Figure 5).

Figure 5

Comparison of fine-tuning methods from Dettmers et al. (2023, Figure 1, CC4.0). Full-precision fine-tuning updates the model's weights directly. LoRA fine-tuning trains small extra weight matrices while keeping the full-precision weights fixed. QLoRA stores the full-precision weights in a compact form and uses memory-efficient paged optimizers.

LoRA fine-tuning was first shown by Hu et al. (2021). It freezes the weights of the pre-trained model, so they do not change. It then adds small, trainable extra parts, called rank decomposition matrices, to chosen layers of the transformer. Because fewer parameters can be trained for the new task, LoRA should in theory lower the computing cost of fine-tuning. Hu et al. (2021) showed this with a GPT-3 175B model, which has 175 billion parameters. Fine-tuned with the Adam optimizer (a common method for adjusting weights) and LoRA, it had 10,000 times fewer trainable parameters and needed 3 times less GPU memory. It also did as well as, or better than, standard fine-tuning on several test collections (Hu et al., 2021).

QLoRA fine-tuning was designed to cut the computing cost even further without losing performance. It was first shown by Dettmers et al. (2023). QLoRA stores the pre-trained weights in a compact form called 4-bit NormalFloat, which is a type of number that uses only 4 bits. In theory, this is the best type for this kind of storage (Dettmers et al., 2023). QLoRA also uses paged optimizers. These avoid sudden jumps in memory use that happen when the model processes mini-batches of long sequences (Dettmers et al., 2023). QLoRA has been shown to match the performance of full-precision fine-tuning and LoRA fine-tuning on several test collections (Dettmers et al., 2023).

3.5

Training across several computers

To spread the training work across several computers, we used a two-node cluster for the search of training settings. The cluster ran Rancher 2.0 Community Edition (Rancher, 2024), a tool for managing Kubernetes, a system that runs many small computer jobs at once. Each computer in the cluster had two Intel Xeon Platinum 8480+ processors, 2 TB of RAM, four NVIDIA 80 GB H100 GPUs, and NVMe solid-state storage, a very fast kind of storage.

We trained each design of FLAN T5 on the Query DSL dataset made with DSS. We sent the fine-tuning jobs to Ray Train, a tool for running training jobs, set up for Distributed Data Processing through the Accelerator API (Team, 2023).

We split the training dataset in an 80/20 ratio. The 80% was used for training, and the 20% was held back for checking the models. Every search of training settings used the same split. We trained the models for 100 epochs, where one epoch is one full pass through the training examples, and we checked the models after each epoch. We tracked the evaluation loss, a score of how wrong the model's predictions are, and lowered the learning rate after 10 epochs with no improvement. We calculated the loss following Hsieh et al. (2023):

Llabel=1N∑i=1Nl(f(xi),yi) (1)

Here, Llabel is the loss for predicting the answers, and l is the cross-entropy loss between the predicted tokens xi and the answer tokens yi. A token is one word or piece of a word, and cross-entropy is a standard way to measure how far a model's guesses are from the correct ones.

We also treated the learning as a multi-task problem, as Hsieh et al. (2023) did. This means the model learns to predict not only the answers but also the explanations for each input:

Ltotal=α(Llabel)+(1-α)(Lrationale) (2)

Here, Ltotal is the combined loss, which adds together Llabel, described above, and Lrationale:

Lrationale=1N∑i=1Nl(f(xi),ri) (3)

This is the cross-entropy loss between the predicted tokens xi and the explanation ri for the answer. In Equation 2, alpha (α) was an extra training setting that controlled how much the model's loss came from predicting explanations. We set alpha to 0.5, so that the loss from predicted explanations and the loss from predicted answers counted equally.

3.6

Searching for the best training settings

Table 2 shows the training settings that we used in every search. We based the learning rate on the best results Hsieh et al. (2023) found for the T5 designs. The batch size is the number of training examples handled at one time across all the computers. In our cluster, each of the 8 computers handled one example per batch, so the total batch size was 8 training examples per batch. As shown in Equation 2, we set alpha to 0.5 to balance the loss from explanations and the loss from answers.

Table 2

Training settings used in every fine-tuning run, not counting the model design.

| Hyperparameter | Value

| Learning rate | 5e-5

| Learning rate patience | 10 epochs

| Learning rate factor | 1e-1

| Number of epochs | 100

| Total batch size | 8

| Alpha | 0.5

Total batch size is the number of training examples per batch across all computers.

For LoRA and QLoRA, we kept two settings the same in every search: the target modules and the dropout rate. Target modules are the parts of the model that the extra LoRA/QLoRA parts attach to. We chose them based on the performance reported in Dettmers et al. (2023). The dropout rate (Srivastava et al., 2014) is the chance that a part of the model is switched off during training, which helps the model learn more robustly. We chose it based on the performance points made in Lin et al. (2024).

The other settings we searched were the LoRA and QLoRA rank and alpha. The rank sets the size of the LoRA/QLoRA matrices (Hu et al., 2021). The alpha is a scaling factor that sets how strongly the LoRA/QLoRA matrices change the original model's weights (Hu et al., 2021). For each rank, we tried a series of alpha values. We tested ranks of 32, 64, and 128. With rank 32, we tried alphas of 32, 64, and 128. With rank 64, we tried 32, 64, 128, and 256. With rank 128, we tried 32, 64, 128, 256, and 512. This gave alpha-to-rank ratios of 1:4, 1:2, 1:1, 2:1, 3:1, and 4:1. We used them to find out whether there is a best alpha-to-rank ratio.

The search included 86 runs of training settings, spread across all three fine-tuning methods and all four model designs. For each set of settings, we tried a fine-tuning run for every model design and every fine-tuning method, starting with the smallest model. If a run succeeded, we moved on to the next model design, in order of increasing size. We kept going until the models would no longer run because the cluster's GPUs ran out of memory. When that happened, we switched to the next fine-tuning method and repeated the process with the same settings, again starting with the smallest model. Once we had tried every fine-tuning method and every model size for a set of settings, we changed the settings and started the whole process again.

In total, we ran 3 runs with full-precision fine-tuning, 39 runs with LoRA, and 44 runs with QLoRA. We ran 29 searches with the FLAN T5 Small design, 29 with FLAN T5 Base, 29 with FLAN T5 Large, and 5 with FLAN T5 XL. Because of limits on GPU memory, all the FLAN T5 XL runs used QLoRA. The whole search took 499.6 hours of computing time.

3.7

How we tested the effect of the explanations

To measure how much the DSS explanations help with the task, we ran a comparison that left one part out. We compared two versions of the loss in Equation 2. In the first, called rational-augmented supervision (alpha = 0.5), the model is checked on both its answers and its explanations, and each counts equally toward the total loss. In the second, called label-only supervision (alpha = 1.0), the loss from the explanations is ignored while the model is trained. We kept all other training settings the same, so that any difference in performance could be put down only to whether or not the model was trained on the explanations.

This comparison covered all three fine-tuning methods and three model sizes: FLAN-T5 Small, Base, and Large. We chose these models to cover the range of model sizes while still letting us compare all the methods, given our limits on computing. Each run used the same dataset and the same training-and-checking split as the full experiments. We ran each one twice, each time with a different random seed, which is the starting point for the model's random choices. We then averaged the two results, to reduce the ups and downs that come from these random starting points.

3.8

How we judged the results

For the final comparison, we used the best evaluation loss reached in each search of training settings. We tested the fine-tuned student models from all the methods on the same checking data. We also compared the computing cost of each fine-tuning method, using the training samples per second and the total training time for each model and method. These numbers were recorded by the Rancher Kubernetes cluster.
parts.results:
4

Results

We start with Figure 6, which shows the average results of our search of training settings for each model and each fine-tuning method. The bottom-left chart shows the average amount of memory used on the graphics cards (GPUs) for each model type and fine-tuning method.

For the FLAN-T5 Small and FLAN-T5 Base models, full-precision fine-tuning used the most memory on average, followed by LoRA and then QLoRA. The FLAN-T5 Large model behaved differently. There, full-precision used the least memory on average, followed by QLoRA, and LoRA used the most.

In every fine-tuning method, the average memory used went up as the model got bigger. But the rate of that rise was clearly different for LoRA and QLoRA than for full-precision. Going from FLAN-T5 Base to FLAN-T5 Large, full-precision memory use grew only a little. LoRA and QLoRA, on the other hand, used more than twice as much memory on average when training the FLAN-T5 Large model as when training the FLAN-T5 Base model.

Figure 6

The four charts show, for each model and each fine-tuning method, the average computing cost and the average evaluation loss.

The top-right chart in Figure 6 shows another measure of computing cost: the average number of training examples processed per second for each model and fine-tuning method. This is the total number of training examples handled by all the computers in our cluster each second, not the number handled by each computer alone.

With the FLAN-T5 Small model, full-precision had the highest average, with LoRA second and QLoRA third. As the models got bigger, every fine-tuning method processed fewer examples per second on average, but full-precision dropped the most. With the FLAN-T5 Base model, LoRA had the highest average, full-precision came second and QLoRA came third. With the FLAN-T5 Large model, full-precision had the lowest average, LoRA had the highest and QLoRA was in between. Notably, the FLAN-T5 XL model run with QLoRA processed slightly more examples per second on average than the FLAN-T5 Large model runs.

The number of examples per second gives a close-up view of how efficiently training runs. But the average total time of a single search of training settings gives a better estimate of the total computing cost of training a model.

The bottom-right chart in Figure 6 shows that average total time, in seconds, for each model and fine-tuning method. Full-precision training time rose quickly as the model grew. It was the fastest method on average with FLAN-T5 Small, the second-fastest with FLAN-T5 Base, and the slowest with FLAN-T5 Large. LoRA and QLoRA showed smaller, steadier increases. For both of them, the average training time roughly doubled between FLAN-T5 Base and FLAN-T5 Large. QLoRA also took a little longer on average with FLAN-T5 XL than with FLAN-T5 Large.

Why did LoRA and QLoRA take longer on average than full-precision for the smaller models? During training, the model runs two passes over the data. In the forward pass, it works out its answer. In the backward pass, it works out how to adjust itself to get closer to the right answer. LoRA and QLoRA need extra work for these passes. They must handle the small extra parts they add to the model, called adapter matrices. QLoRA must also convert its compact 4-bit model back into a more detailed form, a step called dequantization, during both passes. Full-precision does not need this extra work. However, because it updates the whole model, tuning it costs more overall, so it takes longer to train the larger models.

The top-left chart in Figure 6 shows the average evaluation loss for each model and fine-tuning method. Evaluation loss is a score of how wrong a model's answers are, so lower is better. These averages cover the whole search of training settings for each model and method.

The fine-tuning methods kept the same order of performance across all the model types. On average, the full-precision models did better than the LoRA and QLoRA models, and the QLoRA models did worse on average than the LoRA models. Looking at all four charts together, for the FLAN-T5 Small and FLAN-T5 Base models, full-precision gave better performance and faster training on average than the other methods, at the cost of using more GPU memory.

For the FLAN-T5 Large model, however, full-precision used less GPU memory on average than LoRA and QLoRA. This may seem surprising, because LoRA and QLoRA are designed in theory to use less memory. But the result matches earlier research (He et al., 2022).

In practice, these methods add extra memory in several ways. First, full-precision only updates the model's original numbers. LoRA adds extra small parts that can be trained. These are small compared with the original model, but they still add numbers and extra bookkeeping information, called optimizer states, that must be stored in memory. This memory cost grows with the number of layers in the original model. The FLAN-T5 Large and XL models have twice as many layers as the FLAN-T5 Base model (see Table 1). During the forward and backward passes, the model keeps these LoRA numbers and optimizer states in memory on top of the original model, so it uses more memory than full-precision fine-tuning.

Next, QLoRA stores the original model in a compact 4-bit form during training. But during the forward and backward passes, it has to convert those 4-bit numbers back into a more detailed form called half-precision (FP16) (Dettmers et al., 2023). Together with the LoRA memory cost described above, this may help explain why QLoRA used more memory for the FLAN-T5 Large and XL models.

Differences in how the methods are built could be another reason for the extra memory. Full-precision uses the standard PyTorch libraries (PyTorchFoundation, 2025) for training. The other methods use the Hugging Face Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) library (HuggingFace, 2025b) and the bitsandbytes library (HuggingFace, 2025a). These may not be as well tuned for memory as the standard PyTorch libraries.

Now we turn from computing costs to performance. Figure 7 shows how performance changed with two LoRA settings, the rank and the alpha, for both LoRA and QLoRA. It shows the average evaluation loss, across all model types, for each combination of rank and alpha.

On average, LoRA did better than QLoRA at higher rank and alpha values, except for rank 64 with alpha 256. Interestingly, the average evaluation loss went down as the rank and the alpha went up. For any given rank, the best average performance came when the alpha was as large as possible. In fact, the best average performance for any given rank came when the alpha was set to four times the rank.

These observations show that, for QLoRA, performance is strongly linked to higher rank and alpha, and, for QLoRA in particular, to a higher alpha-to-rank ratio. We also saw no crossover point: we never found a case where a higher rank, a higher alpha, or a higher alpha-to-rank ratio gave worse average performance than lower values of those settings.

Figure 7

Average evaluation loss for each combination of rank and alpha, for the LoRA and QLoRA fine-tuning methods across all model types.

We ranked the eight best fine-tuned models by evaluation loss (see Table 3). For each one, the table also shows the model type, the LoRA alpha and rank (where used), the GPU memory used, and the total training time.

The best model was the FLAN-T5 Large model trained with full-precision. It used the second-least GPU memory during training, but it took the longest to train. LoRA and QLoRA are designed to use less GPU memory, yet Table 3 and Figure 6 show the opposite. To train the best model type, the FLAN-T5 Large, LoRA and QLoRA needed much more memory than full-precision.

The one exception to this pattern was the FLAN-T5 Large model trained with LoRA, with a rank of 128 and an alpha of 512. Of the top eight models, it used the least GPU memory to train. It also processed the second-highest number of training examples per second and had the second-shortest total training time.

Among the top-performing LoRA and QLoRA models, the rank-to-alpha ratio was, with two exceptions, either 2:1 or 4:1. Another pattern is that every LoRA model took much less time to train than the QLoRA models, while the QLoRA models tended to use less GPU memory than LoRA. This fits with the differences in how the two methods are built. QLoRA converts the base model back into a more detailed form during the forward and backward passes, which adds extra training time.

The FLAN-T5 Large model also dominated the top eight, and the FLAN-T5 XL appeared only once, in third place. LoRA appears five times in the top eight, QLoRA twice, and full-precision only once.

5

Discussion

In this work, we tested how well three ways of fine-tuning (full-precision, LoRA and QLoRA) work across several sizes of the FLAN-T5 model. This showed us the trade-offs between how much computing each method needs, how long training takes, and how well the model does on the task. We also used DSS to build a unique set of training examples efficiently for our task of turning everyday-language questions into Query DSL search commands. Then we ran a comparison that left one part out, to test our idea that the step-by-step explanations help the model learn. Together, these parts show a development process that can grow to handle more work and can be used to put fine-tuned language models into real-world use. It builds on, and adds to, recent progress in efficient fine-tuning and in building training examples (Hu et al., 2024; Oliver and Wang, 2024; Rajabzadeh et al., 2024).

Our experiments and the comparison that left one part out give real-world evidence that our fine-tuning strategy works. More broadly, though, they show that building training examples efficiently and running the training efficiently are directly linked. In the sections below, we look at what the results mean for using models in real production settings. We consider the trade-offs between performance and computing cost, how the approach scales to bigger models and bigger computing budgets, and exactly how much the step-by-step explanations help the model learn the task.

5.1

Trade-offs between performance and computing cost

Table 3 shows clear trade-offs between how well each fine-tuning method and model size performed and how much memory the graphics cards (GPUs) used. To judge performance, we used a score called evaluation loss. It measures how wrong the model's answers are on examples it has not seen during training, so a lower score is better.

Full-precision fine-tuning always gave a lower evaluation loss than the other methods, except for the FLAN-T5 XL model. We could not use that model because we did not have enough resources. But full-precision came at a cost. For the smaller models, FLAN-T5 Small and FLAN-T5 Base, it used much more GPU memory on average. This shows how hard it is to use full-precision fine-tuning when resources are limited, because GPUs often have little memory. Limited GPU memory often stops us from using larger models that might be more capable on a particular problem. In our case, it did stop us (Figure 6).

This extra memory cost is balanced out, however, by the fact that full-precision needed fewer training runs to find the combination of training settings that beat the other methods. So although full-precision may cost more GPU memory up front, the smaller number of runs makes the whole search for training settings cheaper in total computing time. This shows that full-precision is the most efficient and suitable method in two kinds of settings: where the computing power of the GPUs is not a limit, and where time is a limit.

In practical terms, these findings support a way of choosing a fine-tuning method based on the limits of where the model will be used. If the main goal is the best possible performance on the task and the shortest time to develop the model, full-precision is the best choice. If memory is the main limit, and the model must be as large as possible within a fixed amount of GPU memory, QLoRA is a good option. If both time and GPU memory are limited, LoRA is the best choice. So there is no single best method. Instead, settings with different limits benefit from different fine-tuning methods.

5.2

Scaling up to bigger models

When GPU resources are the main limit, LoRA and QLoRA use memory more efficiently than full-precision fine-tuning for the smaller models, such as FLAN-T5 Small and FLAN-T5 Base. We saw this by comparing evaluation loss with memory use. DSS cuts the work needed to build a high-quality set of training examples. Combined with DSS, these methods offer practical solutions for real-world fine-tuning where GPU resources are the main limit. Our process, DSS plus LoRA or QLoRA fine-tuning, cuts the time to build the examples, the complexity of the examples, and the memory used, all at once. This makes it possible to quickly put fine-tuned language models for specific tasks into use on devices with little memory or on smaller cloud computers.

These methods saved less memory as the models got bigger. With the FLAN-T5 Large model, LoRA and QLoRA used much more memory on average than full-precision. But QLoRA was the only method that let us fine-tune the FLAN-T5 XL model with the resources we had. So QLoRA offers a way to fine-tune large models on smaller groups of computers and on smaller devices, while giving up only a reasonable amount of performance compared with full-precision. DSS adds to this by letting us build training examples efficiently that are well suited to fine-tuning. This further cuts the total time needed to reach strong performance on specialized tasks. In practice, using our strategy with QLoRA will make it possible to fine-tune large models in settings with little memory.

We also looked at how many training examples each method could handle per second. QLoRA did slightly better than LoRA on the FLAN-T5 XL model, but not on the FLAN-T5 Large model (Figure 4). This shows that the improvements QLoRA is designed to make over LoRA, such as storing the model's numbers in a compact form and using a memory-management trick called paged memory, give real-world savings in computing cost when fine-tuning larger models. But this gain in examples per second comes with a longer average training time for each run of QLoRA. So the benefit of needing less computing is balanced out by using those resources for longer.

We also looked at how the search for training settings scales up. Full-precision fine-tuning searched over 7 training settings (Table 2). We chose these based on earlier research, and full-precision needed only 3 runs to reach strong performance. LoRA and QLoRA needed to search over 4 more settings: the rank, the alpha, the target modules (which parts of the model get the extra parts), and the dropout rate (how often a part is switched off during training). These needed a large number of runs before we found values that matched the performance of full-precision.

When we looked at the LoRA and QLoRA models, we found a strong link between how well they performed and the values of the rank and alpha settings. Higher rank and alpha values led to a lower average evaluation loss. The best performance came at an alpha-to-rank ratio of 4:1. This suggests that raising both settings lets the model learn richer patterns without much extra computing cost. We did not test alpha and rank values that would go beyond that 4:1 ratio. Still, the data gave no sign that raising them further would make the model perform worse or make fine-tuning much less efficient. This suggests that even higher rank and alpha values, and even larger alpha-to-rank ratios, may boost performance further. For this reason, we recommend starting a search for training settings with these methods at an alpha-to-rank ratio of at least 4:1, using the highest alpha and rank values that are possible.

5.3

How the step-by-step explanations affect training

We designed the comparison in Table 4 to pick out the effect of the step-by-step explanations on their own. We compared training with the explanations included (α = 0.5) against training with only the correct answers (α = 1.0), across several model sizes and fine-tuning methods. In all eight setups we tested, training with the explanations gave a lower evaluation loss than training with only the answers. This shows that DSS training consistently improves fine-tuning on the task of turning everyday-language questions into Query DSL search commands.

How much the improvement helped depended on the model size and the fine-tuning method. The biggest drop in evaluation loss came in the setups with the smallest models and the least precise numbers: FLAN-T5 Small, and especially FLAN-T5 Small with QLoRA. The smallest differences came with larger models that used more precise numbers. This suggests that the larger models could learn much of the structure of the task from the questions and the correct answers alone. Taken together, these results show that teaching the explanations gives the model a structured signal to learn from, which helps every model learn more efficiently. The help is greatest when limits on computing keep the model small. Even for the larger models, where the improvement was smaller, the explanations still gave a measurable boost. So the benefit is broad, not limited to small models.

These observations fit with earlier work showing that explanations help models learn more efficiently by giving them a chain of reasoning in between, which structures how they learn (Hsieh et al., 2023). Our study goes further. It shows that teaching the explanations still helps when the model is fine-tuned in a way that changes only a small part of it, and when the model's numbers are stored in a compact form, on a more complex task. Earlier DSS research did not include these conditions. This suggests that DSS explanations do more than help a model handle new examples when it has seen only a few. They are also a tool for helping a model settle on good answers faster when resources are limited.

5.4

Comparing the fine-tuning methods

Of the fine-tuning methods, full-precision performed best and was the most efficient in computing, because it took the least total time to find the best training settings. These strengths make DSS combined with full-precision the most attractive choice for many uses, especially when fast development or a limited computing budget is needed. DSS combined with LoRA and QLoRA gave higher evaluation loss than full-precision. But for most model sizes it used GPU memory more efficiently, and it let us train larger models, at the cost of longer training and a longer search for training settings. This makes LoRA and QLoRA practical choices for tasks where memory is a main concern, or where a long search for training settings is not a worry. Examples include edge devices (small computers out in the field), systems with limited GPUs, and small cloud setups.

Taken together, our performance tests, our scaling-up tests and our comparison that left one part out show that building training examples efficiently and fine-tuning models efficiently both speed up putting fine-tuned models to work on specific tasks. DSS lowers the amount of data needed for every fine-tuning method. The limits of the computing environment then guide the choice between full-precision, LoRA and QLoRA, without changing the basic training process. This means our approach can be used as a set of building blocks. DSS gives a steady base for building training examples efficiently, and the fine-tuning method can be chosen based on the computing available, the model size and the practical limits. As a result, choosing a fine-tuning method becomes a decision about where and how to use the model, rather than something that holds back its performance.

5.5

Limitations

Several limitations should be kept in mind when reading this work, and they could be topics for future study. First, we tested only one task: turning everyday-language questions into Query DSL search commands for one particular data environment. This task is typical of a wider family of problems that turn human language into a formal language. But our conclusions may not carry over directly to other areas, such as writing open-ended text, having conversations, or sorting things into categories, unless they are checked further.

Second, we used only a limited set of ways to measure performance. Our main measure was evaluation loss, calculated word by word (token by token) on a set of examples kept aside for testing. We added measures of computing: training examples per second, total training time and GPU memory use. These are useful for describing how training behaves and how many resources it uses, and we checked every training example for correctness and validity. But they do not directly show whether the model's answers are correct, such as how often the DSL JSON (the structured data format of the search command) matches exactly. Our comparison showed a steady drop in loss when the explanations were included. Even so, future work should add other measures, such as BLEU, METEOR and Translation Edit Rate (TER) scores, which are standard ways of scoring how well one piece of text matches another. These would give a fuller picture of how well the model performs.

Because our computing resources were limited, we could not search for training settings or run the comparison for every combination of model size and fine-tuning method. So our conclusions about scaling up come from only some of the possible setups. In the same way, we averaged the comparison results over a small number of random seeds (the starting points that make each training run slightly different), which may not fully show how much training results can vary. Also, our methods focus on the FLAN-T5 family, which reads text and then writes an answer. They do not include decoder-only models, which read text and only write an answer, and which are common in many LLMs used in production. Our methods can work with decoder-only models with only small changes to the code, but testing them on such models is still an open task.
